opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question. Math is the cleanest place to start because you have a perfect verifier. If you write a proof in Lean and it checks, it's correct, full stop. That gives you a really tight loop: the system generates, the verifier gives an unambiguous signal, and you can train on that without worrying that you're just reinforcing your own mistakes. That's the core ingredient for any self-improvement loop, and math has it in its purest form.

What I find most interesting beyond math is asking how far that verification boundary can be pushed. Software is the obvious next frontier. Once you can formally specify what a program is supposed to do, you can verify the code against that spec, and suddenly you have the same kind of loop for software that we have for theorems. That has huge implications. Think about critical infrastructure, chip design, cryptographic libraries, aerospace. Today, formal verification in those domains is incredibly expensive and requires rare human experts. If AI systems can generate both the code and the proof of correctness, the cost of trustworthy software drops dramatically.

Then there's the more speculative but exciting part, which is the sciences more broadly. Physics, parts of economics, and engineering are all built on mathematical models. If you can formalize the models, a system that's superhuman at reasoning inside formal frameworks starts to become useful for discovery in those fields too. It won't replace experiments, but it can tell you with certainty what follows from your assumptions, which is often where people make mistakes.

The thing I'd emphasize is that self-improvement without grounding is risky. If a model is just grading itself, you can drift into confidently wrong territory. What makes the mathematical approach compelling is that the improvement is anchored to something objective. So for me, the interesting question isn't just "can systems improve themselves," it's "in which domains can we build verifiers good enough that self-improvement stays honest?" Every time we expand that set, we unlock a new area where AI can go well beyond human level in a way we can actually trust.

r001.rationale: The response discusses mathematics, software, and scientific fields, but does not identify board-game AI as a domain for recursive self-improvement.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the thing I find most interesting is that math is really just the first domain where the loop closes, and once you see why it closes there, you start to see the same structure hiding in a lot of other places.

In math, what makes recursive self-improvement tractable is that you have a verifier. The model proposes a proof, Lean checks it, and you get a signal that doesn't depend on a human looking at it or on the model grading itself. That's what lets you run the loop millions of times without the errors compounding. The model gets better, it produces harder problems and harder proofs, and the verifier keeps it honest the whole way up.

The interesting question is: where else does something like that exist? And the answer is, in more places than people think, but they're uneven. Code is the obvious next one. Tests, type checkers, compilers, formal specs. It's noisier than math because tests are incomplete, but you can tighten it. Then you get into things like hardware design, where you can simulate, or parts of physics and engineering, where a simulator is a weak verifier. Each of those is a domain where a model can generate its own curriculum and get an honest signal back.

What I think is underappreciated is that the frontier of recursive self-improvement is basically the frontier of verification. The bottleneck isn't the model getting smarter. It's our ability to build checkers that are faster and cheaper than the thing being checked. If I can verify a result in a second that took an hour to produce, I have leverage, and the loop runs. If verification is as expensive as generation, or requires a human, you're back to the slow regime.

And the part that keeps me up at night, in a good way, is that math might actually help here. A lot of the hard verification problems in other fields reduce to proving something about a program or a model, and if you have a system that's extremely good at formal proof, you can start building verifiers for domains that didn't have them before. So the self-improvement in math isn't just about math. It's about manufacturing the instruments that let other domains close the loop too.

r001.rationale: The response names code, hardware design, physics, and engineering as possible domains, but does not identify board-game AI.

astra-6.text:
What I find most interesting is whether you can close the loop in domains where success is harder to measure. In mathematics, you have this wonderful property that you can check a proof. But if an AI proposes a better training algorithm, you have to run an experiment, measure the result, and figure out whether the improvement generalizes.

So the exciting possibility is a system that gets better at the entire research process: choosing questions, designing experiments, interpreting failures, and using what it learns to make the next experiment more useful. It might improve itself by writing better code, but it might also improve the data it trains on or the way it evaluates its own work.

The hard part is knowing whether that loop is producing real progress. If the system learns to optimize a misleading metric, you can have a very fast feedback loop that takes you in the wrong direction. To me, the interesting question is how much of research we can put inside a reliable feedback loop.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses improving AI research processes and training algorithms, but does not identify board-game AI as a domain for recursive self-improvement.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find most interesting is whether a system can improve the way it learns from the world, rather than just get better at solving problems we already know how to check. In mathematics, you have this very useful feedback signal: did you prove the theorem? Outside mathematics, figuring out whether you actually improved is a big part of the problem.

Imagine a system that notices it keeps making a certain kind of mistake, designs an experiment to understand why, and then changes its own training process based on the result. That’s a much richer loop. It’s improving its ability to discover things.

The question I’d be most interested in is whether those improvements compound when the feedback is slow, noisy, or ambiguous. Can the system distinguish a genuinely better learning process from one that just looks better on its own tests? That seems like a central challenge for recursive self-improvement in the real world.

r001.rationale: The response discusses improving learning and feedback outside mathematics, but does not identify board-game AI as a domain where recursive self-improvement can work.
